newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland honeymoon over for Mowlam.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland honeymoon over for Mowlam.

text.p: If Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, enjoyed a honeymoon with the province's nationalists in her early days in office, she was on Wednesday learning the harsh realities of married life.

The warmth with which she was welcomed in Northern Ireland by nationalists who thought they detected a real change in attitude towards them by the new government in London has now turned distinctly frosty.
With a refreshingly personal touch, Mowlam seemed the antithesis of her rather more remotely patrician predecessor, the Conservatives' Sir Patrick Mayhew.
She has been fighting a benign tumour and at a meeting in Washington after a long hot day she astonished onlookers by removing the wig she wears to hide hair loss caused by her treatment.

The first test of her mettle since she was given the Northern Ireland portfolio by Prime Minister Tony Blair after his landslide May 1 election victory came last weekend and the Roman Catholic nationalist community said she had failed it.
Police chiefs allowed the Protestant Orange Order to stage their annual parade on the Catholic Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
The result was some of the worst violence seen in years and so much criticism of Mowlam from the nationalists that she was forced to speak of her own failure.
"Nationalists are very angry. Nationalists are thinking about whether to talk to me or not so my use may be limited after my failure in Garvaghy. I accept that," she said.

A further storm of nationalist protest burst over her wiith the publication of a leaked Northern Ireland Office document which appeared to show that a decision to allow the Orangemen along the Garvaghy Road had been taken well in advance.

The document, Mowlam's detractors averred, made clear that talks held in the run-up to the march with Garvaghy Road's Catholic residents and with the Protesant Orange Order had been nothing but a sham.
The Irish News, whose readership is overwhelmingly nationalist, said in a editorial: "Mo Mowlam is fast running out of political capital and she knows it."
It poured scorn on her handling of the document -- Mowlam maintains it did not amount to a done deal and has ordered an investigation into the leak -- and concluded:
"The game has come to an end for Dr Mowlam. She must stop playing politics and begin playing straight."
In deciding what to do about Portadown, Mowlam faced a dilemma of the kind she will have to get used to.

If she allowed the march, the nationalists would vent their anger on the streets, as they did. If she banned it, the Protestants would do the same, as one of their paramilitary groups indeed threatened.

It came down to what one her officials in the Northern Ireland office described as "the least worst option", that of "finding the lowest common denominator for getting some Orange feet on the Garvaghy Road".

Martin McGuinness, a top official of the guerrilla IRA's Sinn Fein politcal arm, said: "Mo Mowlam indulged in a pre-conceived plan to deceive the nationalist people of Garvaghy Road by giving the illusion she was engaging in a genuine attempt to find a solution to contentious parades when, in actual fact, she had already made the decision to force the parade through."
Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke, whose country is co-sponsoring Northern Ireland peace efforts with the British government, was also critical.
The Belfast Newsletter, mainly read by Protestants, said it was "gross distortion of fact" to accuse Mowlam of having only one pre-conceived idea of what to do about Portadown.
But Orange Order members were critical of her, saying that if a decision had already been taken, what were the grounds for the prevarication on the issue.
The leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, Ian Paisley, was also angry, saying he had always known the Northern Ireland Office was a "nest of vipers".
Mowlam has learned the hard way that it is almost impossible to please both sides of the province's sectarian divide.
Mayhew was fond of saying: "If you upset both sides in Northern Ireland, you know you are getting it about right. If you upset one side, you are in trouble. "
